units.translation: On the middle of the verse the scholiast noted: "τὰ περὶ τῆς τιμῆς τούτου ὑπὸ θεῶν κέκριται [the matters concerning his honor have been judged by the gods]," who seems to have read not τοῦδ᾽ οὐ διατετίμηται [this man's affairs have not been esteemed] but τοῦδε διατετίμηται [this man's affairs have been esteemed], which Paleius himself proposed, the verb being compounded from διά [through] and τιμάω [to honor], i.e. "I value," as judges are said to ἀγῶνα διατιμήσαι [to assess a contest]. But the sequence of thought must necessarily be as Schuetz explained in his note: "After the herald had said, 'Will you really honor with burial the man whom the city hates?' Antigone replies, 'His affairs have not yet been dishonored among the gods,' i.e., Polynices has up to now been in honor among the gods themselves, so that it is not surprising that I too should honor him. To this the herald replies, 'He has not indeed lacked honor from the gods, before, that is, he exposed this city to danger.'" From this it follows that the verb διατετίμηται is compounded from διά [through] and ἀτιμάω [to dishonor], but since this is hardly probable and the word δυστετίμηται [ill-honored] which Hermann invented cannot be admitted into the passage, I fear that Aeschylus used another verb compounded with διά [through]. The Byzantine scholiast A interpolated the note of the old scholiast as follows: "τὰ περὶ τῆς τιμῆς τούτου τοῦ Πολυνείκους οὐ κέκριται κακῶς , ἀλλὰ τίμιος καὶ οὗτος παρὰ θεοῖς [the matters concerning the honor of this Polynices have not been judged badly, but he too is honored among the gods]." That Abreschius rightly corrected this to "οὐ κέκριται καλῶς , ἀλλ᾽ ἄτιμος καὶ οὗτος [it has not been judged well, but he too is dishonored]" is shown by the same scholiast's note on the next verse: "οὔ , πρίν γε χώραν [no, not before the land]: when Antigone said that the matters concerning the honor of Polynices have been judged badly among the gods, the herald says to her, 'The affairs of Polynices were in no way dishonored among the gods before he harmed the city, but only after he brought evils upon the city.'" Thomas Magister, however, believed that διατετίμηται is compounded from διά [through] and τιμάω [to honor], interpreting it thus: "ἤδη καὶ πάλαι οὐ διατετίμηται καὶ οὐ διὰ τιμῆς ἤχθησαν τὰ τοῦδε τοῖς θεοῖς , τουτέστιν , ἐκ πολλοῦ ἡμέληται οὗτος παρὰ τῶν θεῶν καὶ οὐδεμίαν αὐτοῦ ἐποιοῦντο φροντίδα , οὐ γὰρ ἂν εἴασαν ἐκπεσεῖν τῆς χθονός ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἀδίκως · ὥστε τι καὶ παρὰ τῶν πολιτῶν νῦν μισεῖται . πρὸς ὁ ἀπολογούμενος οὗτός φησιν , οὔ , τουτέστιν , οὐ πρότερον ἠμέληται παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πρὶν εἰς κίνδυνον καταστῆσαι τήνδε τὴν χώραν [already and long ago his affairs have not been esteemed and have not been held in honor by the gods, that is, for a long time he has been neglected by the gods and they paid no attention to him, for they would not have allowed him to be driven out of the land unjustly by his brother; so that now he is also hated by the citizens. In reply to this he says, 'No,' that is, 'He has not been neglected by the gods before he brought this land into danger']."
But will you honor with burial the man whom the city hates (Polynices)?
Already his affairs have not been esteemed by the gods.
No, not before he cast this land into danger.
the matters concerning his honor have been judged by the gods
this man's affairs have not been esteemed
this man's affairs have been esteemed
